# Getting started with Quarto {#sec-outline}

This is a short scaffold for teaching colleagues at Utrecht University how to
build a Quarto book or website. It is deliberately compact: each section below
is one "lesson", with a note on **which screenshot** to capture so the finished
guide is easy to follow along with. The companion chapter
([Tricks from the BMS book](tricks-from-boek.qmd)) shows the more advanced
things you can do once the basics land.

## 1. What Quarto is (and why bother)

Quarto is a free, open-source publishing system. You write in plain text
(`.qmd` files: Markdown + optional live code), and Quarto renders that into a
website, book, PDF, slides, or Word doc from the *same source*. Think "R
Markdown, grown up and language-agnostic" — it works with R, Python, and Julia.

For teaching it is attractive because: everything is text (so it lives in Git
and is easy to co-author), maths renders beautifully, and you can drop in live,
interactive simulations right next to the explanation.

*Screenshot to include:* the [quarto.org](https://quarto.org) gallery page, and
side-by-side a `.qmd` source file next to its rendered HTML output.

## 2. Installing it

Quarto ships *inside* recent RStudio, so many colleagues already have it. For a
standalone install, download from [quarto.org/docs/get-started](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/).
Confirm from a terminal with `quarto --version`.

*Screenshot to include:* RStudio's *About* / version screen showing the bundled
Quarto version, and a terminal showing `quarto --version`.

## 3. Project types: document vs website vs book

The single most useful concept to teach up front. One `_quarto.yml` file at the
project root decides what you are building:

- `type: default` — a single standalone document.
- `type: website` — many pages with a top navbar, good for a course site.
- `type: book` — many chapters with numbered sections, a sidebar, cross-references,
  and a combined PDF. This is what the BMS book uses.

A book *is* a website with extra structure, so it is easy to start as a website
and "graduate" to a book later.

*Screenshot to include:* RStudio's *New Project → Quarto Book* dialog, and the
resulting folder in the Files pane.

## 4. Anatomy of `_quarto.yml`

This is the control panel. Teach it by annotating a real one. A minimal book:

```yaml
project:
  type: book

book:
  title: "My Course"
  author: "Your Name"
  chapters:
    - index.qmd          # the first chapter / landing page
    - intro.qmd
    - methods.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo         # any built-in Bootswatch theme
    toc: true            # table of contents in the margin
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrbook
```

Point out the three blocks that matter: `project` (what to build), `book`
(structure + which chapters, in order), and `format` (how each output looks).
Chapters can be grouped into `part:` sections and can use `text:`/`href:` to
control the sidebar label — see the BMS `_quarto.yml` for a large real example.

*Screenshot to include:* `_quarto.yml` open in the editor with the three blocks
highlighted, alongside the rendered sidebar so the mapping is obvious.

## 5. Writing a `.qmd`: Markdown + code cells

A `.qmd` is Markdown with a YAML header. Teach the essentials: `#`/`##` headings,
`**bold**`, lists, links, and images. Two things worth a dedicated demo:

Maths, using LaTeX between dollar signs — `$\alpha$` inline and `$$...$$` for
display equations. This renders in the browser via MathJax and in the PDF via
LaTeX, from the *same* source.

Live code cells, which run and show their output on render:

````markdown
```{r}
x <- 1:10
mean(x)
```
````

Use `#|` cell options to control behaviour, e.g. `#| echo: false` to hide the
code but keep the output, or `#| label: fig-plot` + `#| fig-cap: "..."` to make
a figure cross-referenceable.

*Screenshot to include:* a code cell in the editor and its rendered output
(a plot), plus a rendered display equation.

## 6. Rendering and live preview

Two commands do almost everything. `quarto preview` starts a live server that
re-renders on save — the fastest way to work. `quarto render` builds the whole
project into `_book/` (or `_site/`). In RStudio both are buttons.

*Screenshot to include:* the **Render** button in the RStudio toolbar, and the
live-preview pane updating after a save.

## 7. Navigation, cross-references and callouts

Show how structure emerges almost for free: the sidebar/TOC is generated from
your chapters and headings; `@fig-cover`, `@sec-intro`, `@eq-growth` produce
auto-numbered, clickable cross-references; and callout blocks
(`::: {.callout-tip}` … `:::`) give you tip/note/warning/important boxes for
pedagogy. All of these are used heavily in the BMS book.

*Screenshot to include:* the rendered sidebar/TOC, a resolved cross-reference
link, and a coloured callout box.

## 8. Theming and styling

The look is set by `theme:` in `_quarto.yml` (pick a
[Bootswatch theme](https://bootswatch.com/), or offer a light/dark pair). For
custom tweaks, add a `.scss` file with a `/*-- scss:defaults --*/` block (to set
variables like `$primary`) and a `/*-- scss:rules --*/` block (for raw CSS). The
BMS book uses exactly this pattern.

*Screenshot to include:* the same page in two themes (light/dark), and the
`.scss` file showing a `$primary` colour change.

## 9. Publishing

Once it renders locally, it is just static files. Easiest routes:
`quarto publish quarto-pub` (free hosting), `quarto publish gh-pages` (GitHub
Pages), or hand the `_book/` / `_site/` folder to any web server (the BMS book
is served from a UU server). PDF output is a single `quarto render --to pdf`.

*Screenshot to include:* the terminal output of a `quarto publish` command, and
the resulting live URL in a browser.

## 10. Where to go next

Point colleagues at the official docs ([quarto.org/docs](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/))
and then at the tricks chapter, which shows how the BMS book embeds interactive
simulations, shares LaTeX macros between HTML and PDF, and controls re-rendering
with `freeze` and `cache`.
